title: Find all employees whose name starts with "A".
shortTitle: Find all employees whose name starts with "A"

s1_definition.profdef: This is a `filter` whose predicate uses `String.startsWith(prefix)`, a method that returns `true` when the string begins with the given sequence of characters. The stream retains only elements whose name begins with the chosen letter.
s1_definition.analogy: The HR clerk at the National Bank of India is told, "Pull the files of everyone whose name begins with the letter A." She flips through the stack and keeps Amit and Anita but puts back Rajesh and Priya. `startsWith("A")` is exactly that first-letter check.

s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** This is a `filter` whose predicate uses `String.startsWith(prefix)`, a method that returns `true` when the string begins with the given sequence of characters. The stream retains only elements whose name begins with the chosen letter.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The HR clerk at the National Bank of India is told, "Pull the files of everyone whose name begins with the letter A." She flips through the stack and keeps Amit and Anita but puts back Rajesh and Priya. `startsWith("A")` is exactly that first-letter check.

**One line to remember:** `startsWith` returns true when a string begins with the given prefix, so filtering on it keeps names with that starting letter.

sections.s2_technical:
The `String.startsWith(String prefix)` method checks whether the string begins with the supplied prefix and returns a boolean. For a single letter you pass a one-character string, for example `name.startsWith("A")`. Inside a stream the predicate becomes `e -> e.getName().startsWith("A")`.

`startsWith` is case sensitive. The capital letter A and the lowercase letter a are different, so `"amit".startsWith("A")` is false. If the requirement is case-insensitive you first normalise the case, for example `e.getName().toUpperCase().startsWith("A")`, which treats both Amit and amit as matches.

Real data often contains null or blank names, which would throw a `NullPointerException` the moment you call a method on them. A defensive predicate guards first, for example `e -> e.getName() != null && e.getName().startsWith("A")`. The null check comes first so short-circuiting prevents the method call on null.

A senior nuance: `startsWith` also has an overload that takes a starting index, `startsWith(prefix, offset)`, which is occasionally handy for fixed-format fields like account codes where a prefix appears at a known position.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India is organising its staff directory alphabetically for a printed annual report, and the editor asks for the section of employees whose names start with the letter A to proof first. The directory is one unsorted list of names from every department. We must pull out just the A-names. This is exactly how filtering with startsWith works — each employee name is tested for whether it begins with A, and only the matches are kept.

The code defines a simple `Employee` with a name. A `DirectoryService` exposes `namesStartingWith(List<Employee>, String prefix)` that filters with a null-safe startsWith predicate. The runnable `Main` feeds a mixed list and logs the A-section.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: Amit, Anita, Rajesh, a null name, and Priya.

Step 1: The stream opens over five employees.

Step 2: Amit enters. Name is not null, and "Amit".startsWith("A") is true, so Amit passes.

Step 3: Anita enters. Not null, starts with A — passes.

Step 4: Rajesh enters. Not null, but "Rajesh".startsWith("A") is false, so dropped.

Step 5: The null-name employee enters. The first test, name not null, is false, so short-circuiting stops before startsWith is ever called — no exception, and the element is dropped.

Step 6: Priya enters. Not null, does not start with A — dropped.

Step 7: `collect` gathers Amit and Anita.

sections.s6_takeaway:
To find elements whose text begins with a particular letter, I filter the stream with a predicate that calls the string method startsWith, which returns true when the string begins with the given prefix. For names starting with the letter A, my predicate tested each employee's name with startsWith of A and kept only the matches.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India this was for the printed staff directory, where the editor wanted the A-section proofed first. The directory was one unsorted list, so I streamed it and filtered on the name prefix. The important detail is that startsWith is case sensitive, so if the requirement had been case-insensitive I would first convert the name to upper case and then test the prefix, which treats both Amit and amit as matches.

A senior point I always raise is defensive handling of bad data. Real banking data has null and blank names, and calling a method on a null reference throws a null pointer exception. So I put a null check first in the predicate and rely on short-circuiting, meaning if the name is null the startsWith call is never reached and the record is simply skipped rather than crashing the whole report. I also made the prefix a method parameter rather than hard-coding the letter A, so the same service produces any alphabetical section on demand.
